description:
Somos SALVEX, un equipo participante del NASA Space Apps Challenge, apasionado por la tecnología, la innovación y la exploración espacial.

Nuestro objetivo es desarrollar una solución de software para monitorear la salud de los astronautas durante las misiones espaciales, ayudando a identificar posibles riesgos y contribuir a su bienestar y seguridad.
summary:
Imagine orbiting the Moon when its surface blocks your signal and you lose contact with Earth for about 40 minutes, as happened during Artemis II in April 2026. Who would detect a medical problem? SALVEX was created to answer that question.

SALVEX is a proposed integrated physiological monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions. It combines three specialized devices: Pulse (heart activity), Vital (movement, physical activity, and temperature), and Breathe (respiratory activity). They send data wirelessly to an external receiver and then to an onboard computing platform. We have already built a graphical interface as our first software prototype.

The platform builds an individual baseline for each astronaut, compares new readings against it, and generates alerts with guidance based on pre-approved medical protocols. Because data is stored and processed onboard, monitoring continues during communication outages, following the “store and forward” principle of NASA’s DTN technology.

This matters because the farther a crew is from Earth, the harder it is to get medical help, a challenge NASA recognizes in its Medical-701 need. SALVEX does not claim to be the first monitoring system, nor does it replace medical professionals. Its innovation is the integration of three specialized modules, individualized tracking, and onboard autonomy. Development is gradual, starting with external-sensor prototypes before any implant research.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

SALVEX is a proposed integrated physiological monitoring system designed to support the health tracking of astronauts during long-duration space missions. It does not just collect measurements: its goal is to turn those records into useful information for decision-making. It works as a four-level architecture in which the levels operate in a coordinated way.

1. Physiological data acquisition. Three specialized biomedical modules each collect a different dimension of the body’s functioning:

  • Pulse: records cardiac activity.
  • Vital: collects information on body movement, physical activity, and temperature.
  • Breathe: records signals related to respiratory activity.

Each device would have specific sensors and an anatomical location that must be determined through biomedical research.

2. Data transmission. The devices send information over a low-power wireless connection to an external receiver unit. This unit acts as an intermediary between the modules and the spacecraft computer: it verifies that data was received and facilitates its transmission. The information is organized with indicators such as date, time, source, and measurement quality, to prevent incomplete or faulty records from being interpreted as real health changes.

3. Computing platform. This application receives the records and builds an individual physiological history. During mission preparation, a baseline is established for each astronaut, meaning a set of reference measurements that shows their usual behavior. This way, the analysis does not depend only on general values but also considers the particular variations of each crew member. The platform also displays charts, compares measurements, and identifies trends.

4. Interpretation and alert module. It identifies trends, persistent variations, and possible irregularities. When the established criteria are met, it generates alerts, presents the related history, and offers recommendations previously approved by specialists. For example, if a pattern is consistent with muscle fatigue or possible cramps, it guides the astronaut on the measures in the mission’s medical protocol and indicates when to request assistance. If an astronaut reports a cramp or breathing difficulty, the application can show relevant instructions, request additional information, and indicate whether an emergency procedure should be activated.

Onboard processing. Data is stored and processed directly on the spacecraft, without depending on a permanent connection to mission control. If communication is interrupted, monitoring continues, and the records that need review by authorized medical personnel are transmitted afterward. This is inspired by the Store and Forward mechanism of NASA’s DTN (Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking) technology. Important clarification: DTN would be used in communication between spacecraft nodes and space infrastructure, not between the implants and the body-worn receiver unit.

Data security. Authentication, encryption, and temporary storage mechanisms are planned to protect physiological information and preserve it during communication interruptions.

What benefits does it offer?

  1. Continuity of physiological monitoring. In some space operations, medical information depends on different instruments and procedures, making it hard to gather all records in one place. SALVEX reduces that fragmentation with three coordinated modules that give a more organized view of each crew member. Its value lies not only in measuring more variables but in relating them to better understand changes during a mission.
  2. Detection of variations that may require attention. A cardiac, respiratory, or thermal indicator can be interpreted differently depending on the astronaut’s condition, measurement quality, and usual physiology. By comparing against an individual baseline, if a persistent and sufficiently reliable variation is identified, the platform generates an alert so the situation can be reviewed before it develops into something more serious. This is a monitoring and support capability, not a guarantee of disease prevention.
  3. Operational guidance when Earth cannot assist immediately. It incorporates a library of professionally reviewed protocols, organized by situation. Its purpose is to facilitate protocol compliance, not to let an algorithm replace medical judgment.
  4. Continuity during communication interruptions. Onboard storage and analysis maintain monitoring when there is no contact with Earth.
  5. Modular development. Each module can be developed and evaluated independently, while the central platform relates the records.
  6. Fewer false alarms. Contextualizing each record prevents an isolated measurement from being automatically interpreted as an emergency.

What is the expected impact?

  • On space exploration: the farther a crew is from Earth, the harder it is to receive immediate medical assistance, maintain constant communication, and have the necessary resources. Microgravity, isolation, and disrupted biological cycles add to this. SALVEX responds to NASA’s Medical-701 need (Human Research Program, Exploration Medical Capability area), which seeks to increase in-flight medical capabilities and enable astronauts to perform medical functions autonomously, given mass and volume limits, scarce supplies, communication difficulties, and few medical evacuation options. It is especially relevant for future lunar and Mars missions.
  • Commercially: it could be marketed institutionally to space agencies, aerospace companies, research centers, and biomedical technology providers. The platform could be offered through licenses, the modules as components that integrate into existing medical systems, and there could also be research, adaptation, and maintenance contracts. We do not present profitability figures because there is not yet a manufacturing budget, research costs, certification costs, or a verifiable demand estimate.
  • Realistic scope: its potential depends on testing demonstrating measurable advantages over existing tools: energy consumption, reduced operational workload, reliability, and integration capability.
  • Phased viability: (1) a prototype with external sensors simulating Pulse, Vital, and Breathe; (2) evaluation of accuracy, transmission, storage, and alerts; (3) study of biocompatible materials, implantable designs, and safety testing. This demonstrates that the computing architecture works without claiming that the implants are ready for astronauts.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software were used?

What is documented in your materials:

  • Software developed: a SALVEX graphical interface that lets users manually enter physiological parameters, view records, and understand how each astronaut’s information would be organized. It is the first software prototype; automatic data input from the devices is the next stage.
  • Planned hardware: commercial sensors, electronic components, and low-power wireless transmission technologies for prototypes of the three modules.
  • Technical references: Human Research Roadmap (Medical-701), NASA’s DTN and SCaN, and NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2 (as a guide for design and future testing; this does not mean the project is NASA-certified).
  • Demonstration: a three-dimensional model representing the complete path, from sensor placement on the body to reception, processing, and display on the platform.

What is missing and you need to fill in (it does not appear in your materials, and I won’t invent it):

  • Programming language and framework of the graphical interface.
  • Software used for the 3D model.
  • Specific sensors or boards, if you have already chosen any.

In what way is it creative?

The creativity is not in claiming that each technology is new, but in their integration. We acknowledge that physiological monitoring already exists in space research (NASA tested, for example, a cardiac monitoring system that reached technology readiness level TRL 5) and that NASA has worked on integrating crew medical information. What is original is:

  • Three specialized modules (Pulse, Vital, Breathe) with their own functions, instead of a single device, allowing independent development and evaluation.
  • Individualized tracking: a pre-mission baseline to contextualize each record.
  • Operational autonomy: primary analysis onboard, with later transmission to mission control.
  • Contextual guidance: not just showing a heart rate or temperature, but explaining what it may mean, with alerts and approved protocols.

Our value proposition is to unite three functions that are often studied separately: physiological data collection, individualized analysis, and support for autonomous action. It still needs to be verified whether this distribution delivers better results than a solution with conventional external sensors.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Technical factors: distance from Earth, communication delays and interruptions (such as the ~40 minutes without contact during Artemis II), and measurement quality so that faulty data is not mistaken for real changes.
  • Physiological and environmental factors: microgravity, isolation, disrupted biological cycles, and individual differences between astronauts.
  • Mission constraints: mass and volume limits, scarce supplies, low energy consumption, and ease of use.
  • Security and privacy: authentication, encryption, and temporary storage.
  • Medical safety: protocols approved by specialists; the system does not replace professionals or medical judgment.
  • Feasibility and ethics: distinguishing between the computing system (achievable as a prototype) and the implants (which require biocompatibility, accuracy, stability, and power safety). Implantation in humans is not proposed without passing those stages.
  • Standards and institutional backing: NASA-STD-3001, Medical-701, DTN, and the HRP.
  • Honesty about originality and profitability: not claiming to be the first, and not promising returns without data.
